questions.solution: The logical negation of true is false.
questions.explanation: Logical negation inverts the truth value of a statement. When applied to true, it becomes false.
questions.common_mistake_notes: Common mistake: Choosing B (true). This fails because negating a true statement results in false.

questions.solution: The logical negation of false is true.
questions.explanation: Logical negation inverts the truth value of a statement. When applied to false, it becomes true.
questions.common_mistake_notes: Common mistake: Choosing B (false). This fails because negating a false statement results in true.

questions.solution: The logical negation of unknown does not change its value.
questions.explanation: Logical operations do not alter the truth value of 'unknown' or indeterminate values.
questions.common_mistake_notes: Common mistake: Choosing A (known). This fails because negating an unknown value does not make it known.

questions.stem: What is the result of ¬('not applicable')?
questions.solution: The logical negation of 'not applicable' does not change its meaning.
questions.explanation: Logical operations do not apply to non-boolean or non-truth-functional statements like 'not applicable'.
questions.common_mistake_notes: Common mistake: Choosing A (applicable). This fails because negating a statement that is not applicable doesn't make it applicable.

questions.stem: Which of the following represents the negation of 'If it's raining, then I'll stay home.'?

choices.A: It's raining and I'll stay home.
choices.B: It's not raining or I'll stay home.
choices.C: It's not raining and I won't stay home.
choices.D: It's raining or I won't stay home.

questions.solution: The negation of a conditional statement switches the antecedent and consequent and inverts their truth values.
questions.explanation: The contrapositive form of the given conditional is 'If it's not raining, then I won't stay home.'
questions.common_mistake_notes: Common mistake: Choosing B (It's not raining or I'll stay home). This fails because it's the inclusive disjunction, not the negation.

questions.stem: What is the result of ¬(p ∧ q)?
questions.solution: The negation of a conjunction (AND) is equivalent to the disjunction (OR) of the negations.
questions.explanation: De Morgan's law states that the negation of a conjunction is equal to the disjunction of the negated terms.
questions.common_mistake_notes: Common mistake: Choosing B (p ∧ ¬q). This fails because it only negates one term, not both.

questions.stem: What is the result of ¬(p ∨ q)?
questions.solution: The negation of a disjunction (OR) is equivalent to the conjunction (AND) of the negations.
questions.explanation: De Morgan's law states that the negation of a disjunction is equal to the conjunction of the negated terms.
questions.common_mistake_notes: Common mistake: Choosing A (¬p ∨ q). This fails because it only negates one term, not both.
